title: Which fish are highest in mercury?

seo.title: Fish highest in mercury and which to avoid
seo.meta_description: FDA/EPA list king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish, Gulf of Mexico tilefish, and bigeye tuna as Choices to Avoid for pregnancy, breastfeeding, and young children because of mercury.
seo.search_intent: Identify higher-mercury fish and understand current U.S. fish-consumption advice.

excerpt: Large, long-lived predators accumulate the most methylmercury. FDA/EPA's Choices to Avoid are king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish, Gulf of Mexico tilefish, and bigeye tuna for people who are pregnant or breastfeeding and for young children.
content_html:
Mercury is not evenly distributed across seafood. Large predators that live for years and eat many other fish tend to accumulate the highest methylmercury concentrations. That is why U.S. advice singles out particular species rather than warning people away from seafood as a whole.

The seven FDA/EPA Choices to Avoid

For people who might become or are pregnant or breastfeeding, and for young children, FDA/EPA list king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish, tilefish from the Gulf of Mexico, and bigeye tuna as Choices to Avoid because they have the highest mercury levels in the chart.

The same agencies encourage lower-mercury seafood because fish also supplies nutrients important in healthy eating. During pregnancy or breastfeeding, their guidance is 2–3 servings totaling 8–12 ounces per week from Best Choices.

How large is the concentration gap?

FDA monitoring data put shark near 0.98 ppm mean mercury and swordfish around 1 ppm. Sardines, by comparison, average 0.013 ppm, and shrimp 0.009 ppm. A mean near 1 ppm is therefore roughly 75 times the sardine mean, even though individual samples within any species vary.

Why predators accumulate so much

Methylmercury enters aquatic food webs and remains in animal tissues. A predator consumes mercury already present in its prey, then keeps accumulating it over a long life. Size is therefore a useful clue, but species-specific guidance is more reliable than judging a fillet by how large it looks at the store.

Tuna is a good example of why species matters

FDA/EPA put canned light tuna in Best Choices, albacore/white and yellowfin tuna in Good Choices, and bigeye tuna in Choices to Avoid. FDA monitoring lists canned light tuna at about 0.126 ppm mean mercury versus roughly 0.35 ppm for canned albacore. The word “tuna” alone is not enough to describe exposure.

The useful rule

Keep seafood varied and favor the lower-mercury categories. If pregnancy, breastfeeding, or feeding young children makes mercury guidance especially relevant, use the FDA/EPA chart by species rather than trying to estimate risk from size, price, or whether the fish is fresh or frozen.

faq.question: Which fish should pregnant people avoid because of mercury?
faq.answer: FDA/EPA list king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish, Gulf of Mexico tilefish, and bigeye tuna as Choices to Avoid.

faq.question: Is all tuna equally high in mercury?
faq.answer: No. Canned light tuna, albacore, yellowfin, and bigeye fall into different FDA/EPA categories.

faq.question: Does a large fish always have high mercury?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Size and lifespan help explain the pattern, but species-specific FDA/EPA guidance is the better tool.
